segments.text: Hey friends, meet him — his name is Arjun. Arjun is a truly great graphic
designer whose work is loved by his boss, by clients, basically by everyone. Many
times, Arjun’s friends suggested to him, “Yaar, you do such good work — you
should start something of your own.” And
one day, Arjun finally decides that yes, that’s enough — now is the time.
“I want to be my own boss and I won’t work for anyone else.
I’ll start my own agency” — with this mindset he begins his own
business, hoping it will give him more freedom
and more money. Obviously, in the beginning he feels scared. But he
takes a leap of faith, quits his job, and starts his business.
In the beginning — boom — he lands three or four good clients, which gives him the
assurance of earning more money
than before, and things start moving in a positive direction. But after
18 months,
Arjun’s life looks something like this: It’s 3:00 in the
morning, and he’s working late into the night because of client pressure.
Some time before this,
he had already missed all those birthdays that he used to celebrate so joyfully.
His health starts deteriorating because of the heavy stress and workload
piled on him, and the worst part is — the designing that once was
so close to his heart, he starts to hate it. And this isn’t just Arjun’s story.
Many people start a business with the mindset that they’ll earn more money
and gain more freedom. But real statistics show that of all new businesses
that start, 20% fail within the first year, 50% fail within five years, and
India’s data shows that even among the businesses that do survive and keep
running, 94% never grow into large businesses or generate big money.
Why? Not because they lack skills, or talent, or luck, or because they don’t
deserve success.
The real reason is simple: this happens because most people, just like Arjun, end
up doing the wrong kind of work — work they shouldn’t be doing —
and they fall into a trap where they never actually get freedom.
But their business definitely makes them their own biggest
servant. If you are also in a similar situation where you’ve become
frustrated with your business, or you want to ensure that this never happens to you
in the future, then pay close attention for the next 10
minutes — understanding this will save you a lot of time and help you
earn more money. In today’s video, I’m going to tell you about the three biggest
traps that business owners usually fall into — and how to escape those traps.
By following a six-step system — and I’m not telling you this from my own
imagination; I’m sharing it with the help of one of my favorite business books.
I’ll also explain how Arjun applied the principles
from this book to turn his life around and became a highly successful businessman.
Plus, if you’re a business owner, I have a very special announcement for
you, which I’ll reveal at the end of the video.
It will be very valuable for you, so make sure you watch the video till the
end. Now, let’s start. To understand how
Arjun ended up in this situation after 18 months, let’s go back to the beginning —
because everything starts with your identity and your mindset. To run
a business, you need three people — or rather, three identities.
What are those three identities — those three personalities? Well,
the first personality is the Visionary. This is the part inside
a business owner that says, “Why should I work for others?
I should start my own agency.
I should build an empire. I should become a millionaire.
There should be many people working under me.” This is the first personality —
the first mindset. The second personality is the Operator, the Manager.
This is the person — or the part of a person — that says, “Wait, wait.
All that is fine… but first tell me: how will we get our first client?
How will we communicate with the client?
What will the onboarding process look like? How will we track timelines?
How will we keep everything organized?” And then comes the third… The Craftsman,
also called the Technician, is the part — or the person — who does the actual work.
For example, in graphic designing, the person who is physically
doing the designing is the Craftsman, the Technician. Now ideally,
it’s best if all three of these people exist separately within a business.
But if there’s just one person running everything, then they will have to handle
all three roles themselves.
And many times, when these
three aren’t handled properly, that’s exactly when all the chaos begins.
This is exactly what happened with Arjun. Sometimes his mind would operate in the
mode of “I want to grow the business big.” Sometimes it would shift to “I need
to learn how to manage the business… the people we already
have are not satisfied.” And in the middle of all this, the craft — the actual
design work that Arjun used to do from the heart — started to get affected, because
he was now trying to manage everything and also focus on vision.
That’s why his craftsmanship — the work he used to do wholeheartedly in his 9-to-5
job — started to suffer. Now he was doing three different jobs, acting
like three different people, and
in this process, instead of gaining freedom, he became his own biggest slave.
And this is where a major problem arises,
not just for Arjun, but for many business owners — especially solo entrepreneurs.
Usually, in them, the most dominant personality is the Craftsman.
80% of their time, these people spend on actual work — on designing. 15%
of their time goes into managing the chaos: talking to clients, understanding
their requirements, handling all
that. And 5% of their time is spent on planning for the future.
This is the 80-15-5 percent rule. Now,
usually, the people who fail are the ones who make a mistake here.
What’s the result of this?
Arjun, who was originally a designer, instead of becoming a business
owner, is still essentially a designer.
He’s just taken on two or even ten times more work on his shoulders.
Whereas successful business owners are the opposite.
They spend 80% of their time working on future growth, 15% managing things, and
only 5% doing the actual work themselves, and that too only if necessary.
Otherwise, they don’t do it either.
So the first lesson to understand is this: if you remain just
a Technician in your business, you will never be able to grow.
You either need to hire Managers and Visionaries,
form partnerships, or apply these three roles yourself.
I’ll explain later in the video how you can gradually do this.
But for now, let’s get back to Arjun’s story.
When Arjun left his job and started his business, he got stuck
in three different traps — the same traps that most business owners fall into.
The first trap was the Comfort Zone Trap.
During the first six months, Arjun was doing everything himself, which
felt comfortable to him.
Designing, talking to clients, generating invoices, communicating with
them, collecting payments — he was handling everything on his own.
And because of this, the quality of every single thing was perfect.
There was a sense of control — a different kind of comfort. But the
problem was that all his energy was going into doing different tasks,
and no matter how much effort he put in, the business wasn’t able to grow.
He couldn’t handle more
than two or three clients, which meant his income was stuck at one level.
In fact, many times his income was even decreasing, because payment
issues would arise. He realized early on that as long as he kept doing all
the work himself, his business wouldn’t grow.
He couldn’t move forward, and he wouldn’t get freedom.
That’s when Trap Number Two comes into play — The Delegation Disaster.
For six months, Arjun struggles a lot and then realizes that
he needs to hire someone.
Even if it means paying money, there has to be at least one person to help him.
So he decides to hire a designer, thinking that now the work
he was doing will be shared — roughly split in half.
But what happens is that the person he hires can’t even do half the quality
of the work that Arjun was doing. Plus, he has to give overtime to manage that
person and spend time correcting their mistakes. This often makes him think,
“Maybe I shouldn’t have hired anyone at all.” “I was fine doing everything
myself.” And this is the second trap that business owners fall into — when they try
to delegate work to someone
else, step slightly out of their comfort zone, but still don’t get freedom.
In fact, they end up having to work even more. Why?
Because they don’t have a system in place.
And while facing this, Arjun also ran into the third trap.
The Personality Business — because Arjun himself was closing clients, talking
to them,
and people loved his work. This was a good thing, but it also created a problem.
Every client would always say, “I don’t want
to deal with your team members, I want to deal with you.
I want the design to come from you personally.”
“I don’t want anyone else’s design because I don’t like their work.”
Now, if you’re thinking that this sounds like a good thing, it actually isn’t.
This is again a ceiling, a trap.
Because as long as you’re doing all the work yourself and everyone insists
on having you personally, you still only have 24 hours in a day.
And this is the problem that Arjun realized.
Even after hiring, Arjun couldn’t scale because people still needed him.
He had thought that by starting a business, he would go on vacations, become
very wealthy.
But now he was getting crushed from all sides, because again, he hadn’t built a
business — he had just created a big job in his own name.
Almost every business owner faces these three traps, and because of these traps,
most small businesses or newly started businesses fail — as you can see in the
data.
But while Arjun was struggling with all these traps, he finally came across
a book.
A business book that someone recommended, he started reading it.
And when he read it, he realized that every single thing mentioned in the
book was happening to him
— the personality aspect, the three traps he had fallen into.
From that book, he learned a very
valuable lesson: you should work on your business, not in your business.
He realized that the problem wasn’t that he was working.
The problem was that he was
focusing on the wrong work. There, he learned about the Franchise Mindset.
And you’ve probably noticed
this too: McDonald’s doesn’t sell the best burgers in the world.
I’m sure you’ve eaten better burgers somewhere else than at McDonald’s.
But still, McDonald’s
earns far more than your local shop or any other burger store.
Why? Because they’ve created systems in such a way that even if new college
students come in, they can hire them to run the store, and
the business will still keep running.
Meanwhile, they focus only on branding.
When Arjun realized this, he understood that he needed to think like a franchise.
Whether or not he actually wanted to run a franchise-model business, at least
in his mind he needed to know: if I want to 10x my business, or open 10
different businesses, or 500, or create copies of my business
and hand them over to strangers, how would I be able to do that?
And for this, he did a mental exercise.
He imagined: if I want to create 500 copies of my business
by next year, would I be able to do it?
Well, the answer he got was obviously no.
Then he asked himself another question: If I stop working on the
business for 90 days, will it run without me?
Well, the answer he got was obviously no.
Then he made the decision that this had to change.
Because from the business book,
he had learned that your business should be able to run without you.
Only then are you
truly becoming a business owner; otherwise, you’re just a bigger employee.
To tackle all these problems, Arjun used a six-step framework.
A six-step system — and this is where all the magic started.
Where Arjun was struggling so much, once he started applying this six-step system,
within the next six months he 10x’d his revenue and took
a vacation for the first time in his life. How?
Well, by following the six steps, starting with the first step: The Brain Dump.
Arjun began by tracking everything for two weeks.
Every single task he was doing — for example, a 9:00 AM client call,
10:00 AM designing a logo, 2:00 PM sending invoices, 4:00 PM another
client call, 6:00 PM posting content — he started writing
down every single thing he was doing, one by one.
Within a few days, he realized that he was handling more than 60 different tasks.
No wonder he was feeling so much stress with all the small tasks.
You can try this too.
If you’re a business owner, start writing down every single thing you’re doing,
at least for a few weeks, to see exactly what work you’re doing day to day.
Then comes Step Number Two: The 80/20 Principle.
Arjun looked at his list and asked himself:
Which 20% of the tasks are giving me 80% of the results?
And when he thought about it carefully, he didn’t get a direct answer immediately.
But after investing
some time, he realized that strategy calls with clients, making high-level creative
decisions, and focusing on team growth were the tasks that were generating
maximum sales and growth.
And then he figured out what to do with the remaining 80% of the work.
Well, he gradually started delegating the remaining 80% of the work to others.
He reviewed everything and asked himself again: Can this work happen without me?
If yes, then he delegated it.
Then came Step Three: Document Like a Teacher.
Arjun chose a simple task, such as the client onboarding process, to start with.
He opened a Google Doc and started writing everything down step by step — what
he does to onboard a client. Step 1: Get the client to fill out a form.
Step 2: Send them a welcome email. Step 3: Schedule a meeting with them.
He wrote down all the steps one by one, adding as much detail
as possible, including pictures and screenshots.
Then came Step Four: Test and Refine.
He created such a document and then gave it to his
employee, a junior designer, asking them to follow it.
When the junior
followed it, he realized that there were still many mistakes and problems,
so he started improving the document based on the feedback from his junior.
Then came Step Five, where he decided: just like he had created a
document for onboarding… In the same way, he decided to create a document for every
task he was doing — like the design workflow, revision requests,
invoice generation, social media posting, team meetings.
He started making a business playbook for each task.
The process was very slow, very tiring, and very boring.
Many times, he felt like he shouldn’t even do it.
But still, he made sure that he would keep doing this for at least
six months, no matter what.
And for six months, he did it, which resulted in the creation
of 24 such documents that started systemizing his business.
Then he did the
most important thing: Step Six — Hire for the systems, not for the heroes.
Usually, business owners face this problem — which Arjun was also facing
— that they become
the hero of their own business, and everyone is dependent on them.
But now he had created a system such that even if he brought in a beginner
and just asked them to follow
one document step by step, the beginner would start producing work at his level.
Not exactly like him, but good enough to keep things running.
He spent another six months working on this,
and this is when he truly achieved freedom for the first time.
For the first time in his life, he took a one-week vacation and actually went.
During that time, the two or three people working under him handled
all the business operations, and he was finally able to step away without worry.
